items.prompt: Store A ships an empty `<div id="root">` and a JS bundle. Store B ships fully-populated HTML. Why does the phone see Store B's page sooner?
choices: Store B's server is simply a faster computer
Store A requires the browser to download, parse, and execute JavaScript before anything exists to paint; Store B's HTML can be painted as soon as it arrives
Store A uses an outdated framework
Store B's product data is smaller
items.explanation: Client-side rendering makes the browser do the rendering work after downloading and running JS. Server-side rendering does that work once, ahead of time, so the browser only has to parse and paint HTML it already has.
items.reference:
📦 CSR: empty shell + JS bundle
📄 SSR: HTML already filled in

Why: painting HTML doesn't require JS to have run yet; building the DOM from a JS bundle does.

items.prompt:
A page's server response is `
` plus a `
choices: Server-side rendering
Static generation
Client-side rendering — the browser has to run JS before any content exists
Edge rendering
items.explanation: An empty root element with a script tag is the signature of CSR: the server sent no real content, only the code that will build the content once it runs in the browser.
items.reference:
📦 CSR: empty shell + JS bundle
📄 SSR: HTML already filled in

Why: painting HTML doesn't require JS to have run yet; building the DOM from a JS bundle does.

items.prompt: Which best describes what SSR changes compared to CSR?
choices: SSR removes the need for JavaScript on the page entirely
SSR moves the initial HTML-building work from the browser to the server, so real content can paint before any client JS runs
SSR makes the JavaScript bundle smaller
SSR only works for static content that never changes
items.explanation: SSR is about where the initial render happens, not about removing JavaScript. A page can be server-rendered and still ship JS for interactivity afterward.
items.reference:
📦 CSR: empty shell + JS bundle
📄 SSR: HTML already filled in

Why: painting HTML doesn't require JS to have run yet; building the DOM from a JS bundle does.

items.prompt: A docs page's content never changes after publishing. Which approach avoids rendering it again on every visit?
choices: Client-side rendering
Static generation (SSG) — render once at build time and serve the same HTML to everyone
Streaming SSR
Edge rendering
items.explanation: SSG is SSR done once at build time instead of per-request. For content that doesn't change per-visitor, this avoids paying any render cost on the actual request path.
items.reference:
ApproachRenders when
SSGOnce, at build time
SSRPer request

Why: SSG trades freshness for zero per-request render cost.

items.prompt: What's the main trade-off SSG makes compared to per-request SSR?
choices: SSG pages can never contain JavaScript
SSG content is only as fresh as the last build — it can't reflect data that changed since then without rebuilding
SSG is always slower to serve than SSR
SSG requires a database on every request
items.explanation: Because SSG renders once ahead of time, any data change after that build won't show up until the next build (or a targeted rebuild/revalidation). SSR re-renders per request, so it's always current.
items.reference:
ApproachRenders when
SSGOnce, at build time
SSRPer request

Why: SSG trades freshness for zero per-request render cost.

items.prompt: A page's HTML paints real content at 1.2s, but buttons don't respond to taps until 3.0s. Which metric is 3.0s?
choices: Time to first byte (TTFB)
First contentful paint (FCP)
Time to interactive (TTI) — the page can respond to input
None of these track interactivity
items.explanation: TTI is specifically when the page can respond to user input, which requires JavaScript to have run (e.g. finished hydrating). FCP is when content first appears visually, which SSR can achieve without any JS having executed yet.
items.reference:
MetricMeans
TTFBFirst response byte arrives
FCPSomething real is visible
TTIPage responds to input

Why: SSR mainly improves FCP; TTI still needs JS to run.

items.prompt: Which metric is dominated mainly by network round-trips and server-side work, before any HTML has even started rendering?
choices: Time to first byte (TTFB)
First contentful paint (FCP)
Time to interactive (TTI)
None — all three are dominated by client-side JS execution
items.explanation: TTFB measures how long until the first byte of the response arrives at all — DNS, TCP/TLS setup, and how long the server took to start responding, before content or JS enter the picture.
items.reference:
MetricMeans
TTFBFirst response byte arrives
FCPSomething real is visible
TTIPage responds to input

Why: SSR mainly improves FCP; TTI still needs JS to run.

items.prompt: A visitor in Sydney requests a page from an SSR server that only runs in one US region. What does edge rendering change about this?
choices: It makes the JavaScript bundle smaller
It runs the same SSR logic on a server geographically closer to Sydney, shrinking the network round-trip that dominates TTFB
It skips server-side rendering entirely
It only applies to static assets like images
items.explanation: Edge rendering doesn't change how rendering works — it changes where the rendering server physically runs, so distant visitors don't pay a long round-trip just to reach the server at all.
items.reference: Edge rendering = same SSR, closer server. It shrinks network distance, not render or hydration cost.

items.prompt: Which problem does edge rendering NOT directly solve?
choices: Long network round-trip to a distant central server
High TTFB for geographically distant visitors
A large JS bundle that's slow to parse and execute on a cheap phone CPU
Both A and B are solved by edge rendering
items.explanation: Edge rendering only shrinks network distance. It does nothing about how much JavaScript a device has to parse and execute — that's a hydration/bundle-size problem, solved by different techniques like islands architecture.
items.reference: Edge rendering = same SSR, closer server. It shrinks network distance, not render or hydration cost.

items.prompt: What does streaming SSR change compared to plain SSR?
choices: It sends the whole page faster by compressing it more
It sends finished HTML chunks as they become ready instead of waiting for the entire page to finish rendering first
It removes the need for hydration
It only works for static pages
items.explanation: Plain SSR waits for every part of the page to finish before sending anything. Streaming SSR sends completed chunks over the same open connection as soon as each is ready.
items.reference: Streaming sends chunks as they finish; hydration attaches interactivity to HTML already on the page. Different problems, both attack the CSR-vs-SSR gap.

items.prompt: What does hydration do, in plain terms?
choices: It downloads the initial HTML from the server
It attaches JavaScript event handlers and state to HTML that's already visible on the page, making it interactive
It compresses images for faster loading
It converts client-side rendering into server-side rendering
items.explanation: The HTML from SSR is already visible before hydration runs. Hydration is specifically the step that wires up interactivity — click handlers, component state — onto that existing markup.
items.reference: Streaming sends chunks as they finish; hydration attaches interactivity to HTML already on the page. Different problems, both attack the CSR-vs-SSR gap.

items.prompt: Why does the CSR-vs-SSR gap matter far more on a mid-range phone over 3G than on an office laptop over fiber?
choices: It doesn't — the gap is the same on every device and network
Every extra round-trip and megabyte of JS is paid for twice on a slow connection/CPU — once downloading, once executing — while a fast laptop barely notices either cost
Phones can't run JavaScript at all
SSR only works on desktop browsers
items.explanation: A fast connection and fast CPU absorb the download and execution cost of CSR quickly. A slow connection multiplies download time, and a slow CPU multiplies parse/execute time — so the same bundle costs far more in practice for most of the world's actual mobile traffic.
items.reference: The problem statement is specifically about slow networks/devices — that's where rendering strategy has the biggest real-world payoff.

items.prompt: A team argues 'our staging environment on office wifi feels fine either way, so rendering strategy doesn't matter.' What's the flaw in that reasoning?
choices: There is no flaw — staging performance predicts production performance
Staging tests on a fast network/device mask exactly the costs (download + execute time) that scale up on the actual mobile/slow-network traffic real users have
Staging environments can't run SSR
This is only a flaw for e-commerce sites
items.explanation: Testing only on fast infrastructure hides the very gap this unit is about — the costs of CSR scale with network speed and device CPU, so a fast test environment systematically under-represents what most real users experience.
items.reference: The problem statement is specifically about slow networks/devices — that's where rendering strategy has the biggest real-world payoff.

items.prompt: A server-rendered button is fully visible at 1.0s but doesn't respond to a tap until 1.4s. What's happening in that 0.4s window?
choices: The server is still sending HTML
The HTML is done and painted; the browser is still downloading/executing JS and hasn't finished hydration, so no click handler is attached yet
The browser is redrawing the page repeatedly
The button's CSS hasn't loaded
items.explanation: This is the uncanny valley of hydration: HTML painted correctly and looks done, but the JS that attaches event handlers hasn't finished running, so interactions are silently dropped until hydration completes.
items.reference: Looks ready ≠ is ready. HTML painting and JS hydration are separate steps that can finish at different times.

items.prompt: Why is the 'uncanny valley of hydration' a structural consequence rather than a bug in one specific implementation?
choices: Because all frameworks have the same bug in their source code
Because rendering (producing HTML) and wiring up interactivity (running JS) are two separate steps that fundamentally cannot both finish at time zero when JS has to be downloaded first
Because browsers intentionally delay click events
It isn't structural — it only happens with badly written code
items.explanation: Any architecture that sends HTML before JS has finished downloading and running will have some window where the page looks done but interactivity isn't wired up yet — that's inherent to splitting render and hydrate into separate steps, not a specific bug.
items.reference: Looks ready ≠ is ready. HTML painting and JS hydration are separate steps that can finish at different times.

items.prompt: Under plain (non-streaming) SSR, what determines when the browser gets its first byte of HTML?
choices: Only the fastest data dependency on the page
The slowest data dependency on the whole page — nothing is sent until the entire page has finished rendering
The size of the JS bundle
The visitor's screen size
items.explanation: Plain SSR renders the whole page into one HTML string before sending anything, so a single slow query anywhere on the page delays the entire response, even the fast parts.
items.reference:
ApproachFirst paint blocked by
CSRJS download+execute+fetch
Plain SSRSlowest data dependency, whole page
Streaming SSROnly slowest above-the-fold piece

items.prompt: What does streaming SSR change about which dependency blocks first paint?
choices: Nothing — first paint is still blocked by the slowest dependency on the entire page
Only the slowest dependency needed for the above-the-fold chunk blocks first paint; slower pieces elsewhere can arrive later without delaying it
It removes the need for any data fetching before rendering
It moves all rendering to the client
items.explanation: Streaming sends completed chunks as they finish, so a slow dependency only blocks the specific chunk that depends on it — not chunks that don't need that data.
items.reference:
ApproachFirst paint blocked by
CSRJS download+execute+fetch
Plain SSRSlowest data dependency, whole page
Streaming SSROnly slowest above-the-fold piece

items.prompt: An article page has 3,000 words of static text and one 'like' button. Under an islands architecture, what gets hydrated?
choices: The entire page, same as full hydration
Only the like button — the static text is emitted as plain HTML with no client-side component wrapping and never hydrates
Only the static text
Neither — islands architecture disables hydration entirely
items.explanation: Islands architecture identifies genuinely interactive components at build time and ships/hydrates JS only for those; everything else stays static HTML with zero hydration cost.
items.reference: Full hydration walks the whole tree. Islands hydrate only marked interactive components — same visible result, far less JS.

items.prompt: Compared to full hydration, what's the key difference islands architecture makes to a mostly-static page?
choices: It changes what the page looks like to the user
It changes how much JavaScript ships and gets executed, without changing the visible result — only interactive components cost hydration JS
It makes the initial HTML smaller
It requires the page to have no static content at all
items.explanation: The rendered output looks identical under both approaches. The difference is entirely in JS cost: full hydration wraps and walks the whole tree; islands only touch marked interactive components.
items.reference: Full hydration walks the whole tree. Islands hydrate only marked interactive components — same visible result, far less JS.

items.prompt: How does resumability differ from full hydration and islands, in terms of when event listeners are attached?
choices: Resumability attaches every listener immediately, faster than either approach
Resumability attaches listeners lazily, only when a user actually interacts with a specific element, avoiding an upfront hydration pass entirely
Resumability never attaches listeners at all
Resumability is identical to full hydration
items.explanation: Instead of re-running component logic client-side to rebuild state and wire up handlers ahead of time, resumability serializes what's needed to resume and defers attaching a listener until the exact moment a user interacts with that element.
items.reference: Resumability skips the upfront hydration pass entirely by attaching listeners lazily, on first interaction.

items.prompt: What upfront cost does resumability specifically avoid that both full hydration and islands architecture still pay to some degree?
choices: The cost of sending any HTML at all
A big upfront pass that re-runs component logic client-side to rebuild state and attach listeners before the page is considered ready
The cost of writing server-side code
The cost of using a CDN
items.explanation: Both full hydration and islands still do an upfront pass (over the whole tree, or over marked islands respectively) to attach listeners before interaction is possible. Resumability defers that work per-element until actual interaction.
items.reference: Resumability skips the upfront hydration pass entirely by attaching listeners lazily, on first interaction.

items.prompt: A site adds edge rendering but keeps full hydration and a large JS bundle. What happens to time-to-interactive on a slow phone?
choices: It improves dramatically, matching first paint
It barely changes — a smaller network round-trip doesn't shrink how long the JS bundle takes to download and execute on a slow CPU
It gets worse
TTI becomes irrelevant once edge rendering is used
items.explanation: Edge rendering shrinks network distance, which helps TTFB/FCP. It does nothing about bundle size or CPU execution time, which is what dominates TTI on a slow device — that needs a hydration strategy change, not a location change.
items.reference: Edge rendering and partial hydration solve two different halves of the network+device problem — one doesn't substitute for the other.

items.prompt: Which pairing correctly matches a technique to the specific cost it reduces?
choices: Edge rendering reduces JS execution time on the device
Edge rendering reduces network round-trip distance; islands/partial hydration reduce JS execution cost on the device
Islands architecture reduces network round-trip distance
Both techniques solve the exact same problem redundantly
items.explanation: These are two separate levers on two separate legs of the problem: edge rendering attacks network distance (helps TTFB), while islands/partial hydration attack how much JS a device must execute (helps TTI).
items.reference: Edge rendering and partial hydration solve two different halves of the network+device problem — one doesn't substitute for the other.

items.prompt: Put these in the order they happen for a server-rendered page: (i) browser parses and paints HTML, (ii) server runs the component tree with real data, (iii) browser downloads and executes the JS bundle, (iv) hydration attaches event handlers.
choices: (i), (ii), (iii), (iv)
(ii), (i), (iii), (iv)
(iii), (iv), (ii), (i)
(ii), (iii), (i), (iv)
items.explanation: The server renders first, producing HTML the browser can paint immediately (i). Only after that does the browser fetch and run the JS bundle (iii), and hydration (iv) is the last step, attaching interactivity to markup that's already been visible for a while.
items.reference: Render (server) → paint (browser) → JS download/execute → hydration. Painting doesn't wait for JS; hydration does.

items.prompt: In the SSR pipeline, which step happens LAST?
choices: The server running the component tree with real data
The browser parsing and painting the HTML response
Hydration — attaching event handlers and restoring component state
The browser requesting the JS bundle
items.explanation: Hydration is the final step: it depends on the JS bundle having already downloaded and executed, which itself happens after the HTML has already painted. Everything else in the pipeline has to finish first.
items.reference: Render (server) → paint (browser) → JS download/execute → hydration. Painting doesn't wait for JS; hydration does.

items.prompt: Why can the browser paint the HTML response before the JS bundle has even started downloading?
choices: Because painting doesn't depend on JavaScript at all — the browser can render markup it already has as soon as it arrives
Because the JS bundle is embedded inside the HTML
Because painting is triggered by the JS bundle finishing
It can't — painting always waits for hydration
items.explanation: Painting HTML is purely a parsing/rendering step the browser can do the moment it has markup, independent of any JavaScript. That independence is exactly what lets SSR achieve an early first contentful paint even on a slow connection where the JS bundle is still in flight.
items.reference: Render (server) → paint (browser) → JS download/execute → hydration. Painting doesn't wait for JS; hydration does.

items.prompt: Write `fetchBoth(fetchA, fetchB)` that takes two zero-argument functions returning Promises and resolves to `[resultA, resultB]`, kicking off both calls concurrently rather than awaiting one before starting the other (the waterfall bug from the deep dive). Since this sandbox runs code synchronously via eval, implement it using `.then()` chaining or `Promise.all`, not top-level `await`.

tests.description: resolves to [resultA, resultB] in order
both functions are called immediately, before either resolves
tests.expr: (() => { let calls = []; const fA = () => { calls.push('a-start'); return new Promise(r => setTimeout(() => { calls.push('a-end'); r('a'); }, 10)); }; const fB = () => { calls.push('b-start'); return new Promise(r => setTimeout(() => { calls.push('b-end'); r('b'); }, 10)); }; fetchBoth(fA, fB); return expect(calls[0] === 'a-start' && calls[1] === 'b-start').toBeTruthy(); })()

items.explanation: The fix is calling both fetchA() and fetchB() before awaiting either one — that starts both underlying operations (e.g. network requests) at the same instant, so their wait time overlaps instead of stacking. Promise.all then resolves once both have finished, taking as long as the slower of the two rather than the sum of both. The bug this fixes is writing `await fetchA(); await fetchB();`, which doesn't call fetchB() at all until fetchA()'s promise has already resolved — turning two independent, parallelizable operations into a serial waterfall.
items.reference:
await fetchA();
await fetchB(); // BAD: waterfall

await Promise.all([fetchA(), fetchB()]); // GOOD: parallel

Why: awaiting sequentially only starts the second call after the first resolves.

items.prompt: Given the `hydrateIslands`-style pattern from the deep dive, write `countHydratable(nodes)` that takes an array of plain objects like `{ island: 'like-button' }` or `{ island: null }` (representing DOM nodes, some marked as islands and some not) and returns how many have a truthy `island` property — simulating how many nodes an islands runtime would actually hydrate, as opposed to the total node count.

tests.description: counts only nodes with a truthy island property
returns 0 for an all-static page
tests.expr: expect(countHydratable([{ island: null }, { island: null }, { island: null }])).toBe(0)

tests.description: returns 0 for an empty node list

items.explanation: This mirrors the real islands-hydration mechanism: a runtime walks all nodes but only performs hydration work — attaching handlers, restoring state — for the ones explicitly marked as islands. The count of hydratable nodes is independent of total page size, which is exactly why an islands architecture doesn't scale its JS cost with how much static content surrounds the interactive parts.
items.reference: An islands runtime's hydration cost scales with the number of marked interactive nodes, not with total page/content size.

items.prompt: Write `buildChunks(sections)` that takes an array of `{ name, ready }` objects (in the order they'd be rendered) and returns an array of section `name`s in the order a streaming server would actually flush them: every section with `ready: true` is flushed in its original order, and the function stops collecting as soon as it hits the FIRST section with `ready: false` (since a real stream can't flush what isn't ready yet — later ready sections behind a not-ready one still have to wait their turn in this simplified model).

tests.description: returns all names when everything is ready
tests.expr: expect(buildChunks([{ name: 'header', ready: true }, { name: 'body', ready: true }])).toEqual(['header', 'body'])

tests.description: stops at the first unready section
tests.expr: expect(buildChunks([{ name: 'header', ready: true }, { name: 'recs', ready: false }, { name: 'footer', ready: true }])).toEqual(['header'])

tests.description: returns an empty array if the very first section isn't ready

items.explanation: This models the ordering constraint a real chunked HTTP response has: bytes must be sent in order over the connection, so even if a later section happens to be ready, it can't jump ahead of an earlier section that's still pending — the earlier one has to flush (or the connection has to hold) before anything after it can go out. This is why the deep dive's Checkpoint answer notes that reordering which dependency is slow doesn't automatically reorder the flush sequence unless the code explicitly restructures which section is awaited/written first.
items.reference: A stream flushes in write order — a later-ready section can't skip ahead of an earlier section still pending.

items.prompt: Write `wouldMismatch(serverRender, clientRender)` that takes two zero-argument pure functions simulating a component's server-side and client-side first render, calls both, and returns `true` if they produce different string output (a hydration mismatch) or `false` if they match.

tests.description: returns false when both renders match
returns true when renders differ (e.g. window-dependent branch)

items.explanation: A hydration mismatch happens whenever a component's server-side output and its client-side first-render output disagree — commonly from using `window`, `Date.now()`, or `Math.random()` in a way that behaves differently across environments. The fix from the deep dive is rendering the same thing both times initially (e.g. a state default that matches what the server would produce) and only diverging after hydration, via an effect, once both sides agree on the starting point.
items.reference:
// BAD
typeof window !== 'undefined' ? mobileUI : desktopUI

// GOOD: same first render both sides, adjust after

Why: server has no window/localStorage/Date consistency with client on first render.

items.prompt: Write `nextWriteIndex(bufferFull, currentIndex, totalChunks)` simulating a streaming server deciding whether to advance to the next chunk. If `bufferFull` is `true`, it must NOT advance (return `currentIndex` unchanged, representing 'wait for drain before writing more' — the backpressure fix from the deep dive). If `bufferFull` is `false` and there are more chunks left (`currentIndex < totalChunks - 1`), advance by 1. If already at the last chunk, stay there regardless.

tests.description: does not advance when buffer is full
advances by 1 when buffer has room and chunks remain
stays at the last index even if buffer has room

items.explanation: This models the real contract of Node's res.write(): it returns false when the internal buffer is full, meaning the client isn't draining data fast enough. Ignoring that signal and continuing to write anyway buffers unsent data in server memory — under many concurrent slow clients, this is exactly how a single popular streaming page can exhaust server memory. The correct behavior is to pause producing more chunks until a 'drain' event fires, which is what bufferFull staying true simulates here.
items.reference: res.write() returning false means: stop writing, wait for 'drain', then continue — ignoring this buffers unsent data in server memory.

items.prompt: Write `pickStrategy({ contentChangesOften, hasSlowDependency, mostlyStaticWithFewWidgets })` that returns one of the strings `'ssg'`, `'streaming-ssr'`, or `'islands'` following this priority: if `mostlyStaticWithFewWidgets` is true, return `'islands'`. Otherwise, if `hasSlowDependency` is true, return `'streaming-ssr'`. Otherwise, if `contentChangesOften` is false, return `'ssg'`. Otherwise, return `'streaming-ssr'` as the general-purpose default.

tests.description: picks islands for mostly-static pages with a few widgets, regardless of other flags
tests.expr: expect(pickStrategy({ contentChangesOften: true, hasSlowDependency: true, mostlyStaticWithFewWidgets: true })).toBe('islands')

tests.description: picks streaming-ssr when there's a slow dependency and it's not mostly static
tests.expr: expect(pickStrategy({ contentChangesOften: true, hasSlowDependency: true, mostlyStaticWithFewWidgets: false })).toBe('streaming-ssr')

tests.description: picks ssg for content that never changes, isn't mostly-static-with-widgets, and has no slow dependency
tests.expr: expect(pickStrategy({ contentChangesOften: false, hasSlowDependency: false, mostlyStaticWithFewWidgets: false })).toBe('ssg')

tests.description: falls back to streaming-ssr for frequently-changing content with no slow dependency and not mostly static
tests.expr: expect(pickStrategy({ contentChangesOften: true, hasSlowDependency: false, mostlyStaticWithFewWidgets: false })).toBe('streaming-ssr')

items.explanation: This encodes the deep dive's strategy table as an explicit decision order: a page's JS-cost shape (mostly static plus a few widgets) matters most since it determines hydration cost regardless of data freshness; a slow dependency argues for streaming so it doesn't block fast content; and content that never changes can skip per-request rendering entirely via SSG. Real production sites usually combine several of these per page type rather than picking one globally, but a single page still needs one dominant strategy to start from.
items.reference:
SituationDefault
Rarely changesSSG
Slow dependencyStreaming SSR
Mostly static + few widgetsIslands

items.prompt: Write `estimateTTFB({ dnsMs, tcpMs, tlsMs, serverMs })` that sums the four numbers to estimate total time-to-first-byte in milliseconds, modeling the fixed connection-setup costs (DNS, TCP, TLS) that happen before any server-side rendering work can even begin, as shown in the deep dive's time-budget chart.

tests.description: sums all four cost components
returns 0 when all components are 0 (e.g. warm connection, instant server response)
a cached DNS + kept-alive connection removes dns/tcp/tls cost

items.explanation: TTFB is the sum of every fixed connection-setup cost plus how long the server actually takes to start responding. This is exactly why connection reuse (HTTP keep-alive) matters so much in practice: a warm connection skips DNS/TCP/TLS entirely and pays only serverMs, while a cold connection pays all four every single time.
items.reference: TTFB = connection setup (DNS+TCP+TLS) + server response time. Reusing a connection removes the first three.

items.prompt: Which of these is most likely to cause a hydration mismatch?
choices: Rendering a component that reads `typeof window !== 'undefined'` to decide what to show
Rendering a static string that never changes
Using a CSS class name
Fetching data before rendering, on both server and client
items.explanation: `window` doesn't exist during server-side rendering, so a branch keyed on its presence renders one thing on the server and a potentially different thing on the client's first render — a classic hydration mismatch source, alongside Date.now() and Math.random().
items.reference: Anything that differs between the server and client environments on first render (window, Date.now, Math.random) risks a hydration mismatch.

items.prompt: A component calls `Math.random()` directly inside its render function to decide which of two layouts to show. What's the risk?
choices: None — Math.random() is deterministic across environments
The server and client will very likely produce different random values, causing the rendered output to disagree — a hydration mismatch
It will make the page render faster
It only affects CSS, not HTML structure
items.explanation: Math.random() produces a different value on each call, including the server's render and the client's separate first render — so output built from it will very likely disagree between the two, exactly like the window-dependent branch example.
items.reference: Anything that differs between the server and client environments on first render (window, Date.now, Math.random) risks a hydration mismatch.

items.prompt: In the deep dive's raw Node `http` server, streaming works by calling `res.write()` multiple times and `res.end()` once, without setting `Content-Length`. What real HTTP mechanism makes this valid?
choices: HTTP/1.1 chunked transfer encoding — the response length doesn't need to be known upfront
A custom protocol on top of HTTP
WebSockets
It's not standard HTTP; it only works because Node is lenient
items.explanation: Omitting Content-Length lets the server use chunked transfer encoding, part of the HTTP/1.1 spec — the browser reads chunks as they arrive on the same connection instead of requiring the total size upfront. This is the real mechanism frameworks' streaming SSR APIs build on, not a special trick.
items.reference: Streaming SSR is chunked transfer encoding, a standard HTTP/1.1 feature — not a framework-specific trick.

items.prompt: Why does the streaming server example call `res.write()` for the header chunk separately from the recommendations chunk, instead of building one big string and calling `res.write()` once?
choices: It doesn't matter — one call would behave identically
Calling write() as each piece becomes ready flushes it over the open connection immediately, instead of waiting for every piece (including the slow one) to be ready first
Node requires at least two write() calls per response
It reduces the total number of bytes sent
items.explanation: Each res.write() call flushes that data onto the wire right away. Batching everything into one string first would recreate plain SSR's problem — the browser gets nothing until the slowest piece (recommendations, 2.5s) is also ready, even though the header and product info were ready in 80ms.
items.reference: Streaming SSR is chunked transfer encoding, a standard HTTP/1.1 feature — not a framework-specific trick.

items.prompt: A team migrates a CSR app to SSR but adds no partial-hydration strategy. What happens to the amount of JavaScript the browser must execute before the page is interactive?
choices: It drops to zero, since the HTML is already rendered
It stays essentially the same as the CSR version — full hydration still walks and wires up the entire component tree client-side
It roughly doubles
It becomes impossible to measure
items.explanation: Full hydration re-runs the entire component tree client-side regardless of how the initial HTML was produced. SSR changes when content becomes visible (first paint), not how much JS the browser executes to become interactive — that only changes with a strategy like islands or resumability.
items.reference: SSR alone fixes first paint. Time-to-interactive JS cost is unchanged from CSR unless a hydration strategy is added on top.

items.prompt: Which claim correctly separates what SSR alone achieves from what a hydration strategy (islands, resumability) additionally achieves?
choices: SSR alone already minimizes JS execution cost; hydration strategies only affect visual appearance
SSR alone improves first paint by sending real HTML early; a hydration strategy on top of it is what actually reduces the JS a device must execute before becoming interactive
There's no meaningful difference between SSR alone and SSR plus a hydration strategy
Hydration strategies replace the need for SSR entirely
items.explanation: These solve genuinely different halves of the same problem: SSR alone gets content on screen sooner (first paint), while a hydration strategy is what actually cuts down the amount of JavaScript a device has to run before it can respond to input (time to interactive). A team that ships SSR without a hydration strategy still pays full CSR-level JS execution cost.
items.reference: SSR alone fixes first paint. Time-to-interactive JS cost is unchanged from CSR unless a hydration strategy is added on top.
